head: A data centre must now bring its own generation
body_text: Ireland ended its Dublin connection freeze and replaced it with a condition: any new data centre must provide generation and/or storage — on site or nearby — matching the maximum import capacity it is asking for, and that plant must bid into the wholesale market. At least 80% of annual demand must come from *additional* Irish renewable projects; already-contracted PPAs do not count. Six years to deliver, and connection requests are assessed against the specific constrained or unconstrained part of the network they land in.

ref: Order No. 26-239, under the POWER Act (House Bill 3546, 2025)
head: Data centres get their own rate class, at 20 MW and up
body_text: The POWER Act obliges Oregon's utilities to serve “large energy use facilities” — 20 MW and above — under a separate schedule, on contracts of ten years or longer, so that the cost of serving them is not spread across everyone else. The Commission approved Portland General Electric's schedule in Order No. 26-239 on 10 July 2026: data centre customers' rates rose about 29% on average, and every other customer class saw a decrease. Pacific Power's equivalent is pending in Docket UE 463, with a decision expected before the end of 2026; Idaho Power is covered by the Act but has no qualifying data centre customers. This is cost allocation rather than generation, and it is here for the same reason Ohio's tariff is: a regulator has found the load large and distinct enough to price on its own. Pacific Power's schedule is docketed as UE 463, PacifiCorp Advice No. 25-015, Schedule 401, Service to New Large Energy Use Facilities, and as of Oct 15, 2026 the end-of-2026 expectation has an order behind it rather than an inference: Chief Administrative Law Judge Alison Lackey issued Order No. 26-310 on Aug 31, 2026 suspending the tariff sheets' effective date until Dec 31, 2026. The contested case is still in hearings, with an intervention ruling on Oct 7, 2026 and Commission Staff's motion to admit pre-filed exhibits, together with the declaration of Bret Stevens, on Oct 12, 2026, so Pacific Power's rate class is still pending and not approved. Read on the Commission's own eDockets docket sheet, which carries the order numbers, dispositions and filing dates; the orders themselves were not retrieved.

head: A statewide model tariff for loads of 50 MW and up
body_text: The Commission adopted a model tariff framework for large load customers on 30 April 2026 and released the Final Order on 13 May 2026. It applies to customers above 50 MW individually or 100 MW in aggregate, and sets guidance on cost causation for interconnection and infrastructure, deposits and collateral against stranded cost where a project is delayed or abandoned, six-month interconnection study timelines, load ramp schedules, minimum contract terms and exit provisions, a public interconnection queue, and customer self-construction of upgrades. The Commission states the load growth behind it is “driven largely by data centers and advanced manufacturing”. Like Ohio's tariff and Oregon's rate class this is cost allocation rather than generation, and it is recorded on that footing: a regulator pricing data centre load as a class of its own, here as guidance for every Pennsylvania distribution utility rather than one company's schedule. No Pennsylvania metro is mapped on this page, so no capacity or consumption figure depends on it.

head: Above 25 MW, bring your own new clean generation
body_text: Section 5 directs MassDEP to develop protocols ensuring that data centre projects with peak electricity demand above 25 MW have procured sufficient *incremental new* clean electricity generation to meet their annual electric consumption, eligible under the Clean Energy Standard (310 CMR 7.75). By 31 December 2026 MassDEP must stand up an alternative compliance payment, with receipts going to a Ratepayer Protection Fund that offsets supply costs for everyone else. Section 3 tells the Department of Public Utilities to keep other ratepayers off the cost of distribution upgrades driven by data centre demand; Section 4 tells it to clear speculative projects out of the interconnection queue using fees and deposits. The same instrument as Ireland's, reached independently: the load is permitted, but only against generation that would not otherwise have been built.

body: Delaware General Assembly, signed by the Governor
head: Large loads must secure 100% of their own power
body_text: Four energy bills signed together, all effective immediately. House Bill 445 imposes a bring-your-own-generation requirement on large energy-use facilities: they must produce or secure 100% of the power they need, including a share of clean and renewable energy. House Bill 233 puts them in a rate class of their own, liable for the full cost of the infrastructure they require rather than shifting it to residential and small-business customers, and first to be disconnected in a grid emergency unless they are self-generating. House Bill 310 removes their access to job-creation tax credits and licence fee reductions; Senate Bill 326 limits the non-mandatory utility capital spending recoverable from standard residential ratepayers. No Delaware market is mapped on this page — the filing is here because it is the same instrument appearing in a third jurisdiction.

head: 9,985 MW approved, about 80% of it for data centers
body_text: Georgia Power's own load forecast for large loads moved from 400 MW in 2022 to 6,600 MW in 2023 to 8,500 MW in 2025. The Commission approved roughly 9,985 MW of new resources — three combined-cycle gas units (Bowen 7–8, Wansley 10–11, McIntosh 12), nine standalone battery projects, solar-plus-storage, and 2,821 MW of purchase agreements. Conditions attached: large-load customers must produce at least $8.50 a month of downward pressure on a typical 1,000 kWh residential bill across 2029–31, Georgia Power eats the cost through 2031 if the contracts underperform, and every new data center contract goes to the Commission 30 days before signing.

head: Three new gas plants built for one customer
body_text: The Commission approved Entergy Louisiana building three combined-cycle gas facilities — two in Richland Parish online late 2028, one at the Waterford site in St. Charles Parish by end-2029 — plus new transmission and up to 1,500 MW of solar procurement, explicitly to serve Meta's Richland Parish campus. Entergy states Meta pays its share so other customers are not exposed. This is the clearest single case on the map of a data center causing power plants to exist.

head: Rules written for plugging a data center straight into a power plant
body_text: FERC directed PJM — the grid serving the largest data center market on Earth — to write transparent tariff rules for large loads co-located with generating facilities, including two new transmission products (Firm and Non-Firm Contract Demand service), interim non-firm service while upgrades are built, and revised behind-the-meter generation rules. A reliability report was due 19 January 2026.

head: Every grid operator told to justify how it connects large loads
body_text: Show cause orders to all six regional transmission organisations at once, giving each 60 days to justify or reform the tariffs governing large load interconnection. One of the reform categories is accommodating co-location agreements and behind-the-meter generation — the arrangement by which a data centre plugs into a power station rather than the grid. This generalises the December 2025 order that directed PJM alone to write those rules, and it is the clearest signal yet that co-location is being treated as ordinary interconnection business rather than an exception.

head: Data centres to get reliability standards of their own
body_text: The Commission directed NERC to develop and submit new or modified Reliability Standards addressing the reliability risks of integrating computational loads into the Bulk-Power System, and to revise its Rules of Procedure including the registry criteria for computational load entities. Both are due by 31 December 2026. No megawatt threshold is set in the order. This is a reliability obligation, not a generation requirement, and it is recorded here on the same footing as Texas SB6: a regulator treating data centre load as a distinct class with duties of its own. It completes the 2026 federal thread alongside the June show cause orders — those govern how the load connects, this governs how it must behave once connected. Nothing on this page depends on it; no capacity or consumption figure moves.

head: Pay for 85% of what you reserved, whether you use it or not
body_text: The first data-center-specific tariff of its kind in the US. Any new or expanded load above 25 MW (or a mobile data center above 1 MW) must pay a minimum bill of at least 85% of contracted capacity regardless of consumption, over a four-year ramp, with an exit fee equal to three years of those minimum charges, plus creditworthiness and collateral tests and load study fees of $10,000–$100,000. Written to stop speculative interconnection requests from stranding costs on everyone else.

head: Large loads must be curtailable — and must declare their backup generation
body_text: Loads of 75 MW or more interconnecting after 31 December 2025 must install equipment allowing ERCOT to curtail them directly during firm load shed. Critically for this map: a customer must disclose whether it holds backup generation equal to at least half its proposed load that cannot export to the grid, and ERCOT may then order it either to run that generation or to shed load during an emergency. Transmission screening studies cost the applicant at least $100,000.

body: Joint Legislative Audit and Review Commission
head: Unconstrained demand doubles in ten years
body_text: Virginia's electricity demand was essentially flat from 2006 to 2020. The legislature's own audit body found that unconstrained demand is now on track to double within a decade, driven primarily by data centers, with the Dominion zone growing 5.5% a year. Meeting even half of that would need solar added at twice the 2024 rate and wind beyond the capability of every offshore site available. A typical Dominion residential customer is estimated to face $14–$37 more per month in real generation and transmission costs by 2040.

ref: Air permit, and appeal to the Air Pollution Control Board
head: 35 turbines installed, 15 permitted
body_text: xAI ran gas turbines at its Memphis campus before holding permits for them. The county subsequently issued a permit for 15, treating them under the Clean Air Act's exemption for 'nonroad engines'. The NAACP, Southern Environmental Law Center and Earthjustice appealed, arguing turbines of that size do not qualify for the exemption and that the facility should have been permitted as a major modification rather than a new minor source. The dispute is about whether on-site generation for a data center is a power plant in the eyes of the Clean Air Act.

head: 252 GW of gas in development, a third of it for data centers on site
body_text: Not a regulator, but built from permit and filing records. US gas capacity in development nearly tripled during 2025 to 252 GW — about a quarter of the world's total — and more than a third of it is slated to power data centers directly on site. In Texas, 40 GW of the 80.6 GW in development is dedicated to data centers.

body: Imperial Irrigation District Board of Directors
head: First to be cut off, on a fifteen-year commitment
body_text: Schedule LL took effect Sep 15, 2026 on a unanimous board vote, after a public review that drew 243 comments and changed the draft. It binds any customer with a monthly expected demand of 20 MW or more and an expected load factor above 80 percent, which is the shape of a data center, and the District may aggregate facilities under common ownership, shared electrical infrastructure or common control to reach that threshold. Service is full requirements at 69 kV or higher and interruptible at the District's sole discretion, and the tariff states the District may interrupt Schedule LL customers ahead of every other rate schedule, with no compensation and no liability for the damages that follow. The customer carries the cost: actual study costs, property rights and permitting, substation and transmission upgrades, a cash Service Deposit of at least three months of its highest estimated monthly charges, an Initial Contract Term of not less than fifteen years with sixty months' notice to leave, an Exit Fee equal to the remaining Minimum Charge, and a monthly energy charge that is the higher of actual consumption or 85 percent of contracted energy. The clause that belongs on this page is co-location: where a Schedule LL applicant proposes to co-locate with a generation resource, the District studies the load and that generation jointly, at the customer's expense. Imperial Valley has no mapped metro here, so no capacity or consumption figure depends on it. It is recorded as the same instrument as Ohio, Oregon, Pennsylvania and Delaware, reached this time by a publicly owned utility's own board rather than a state regulator. Read on the tariff itself, which dates the effective day Sep 15, 2026 and corrects the Sep 16 date the news block carried from a press account.

ref: Docket RM26-4-000, advance notice of proposed rulemaking
head: The directive the federal thread started from
body_text: The Secretary of Energy, acting under section 403 of the Department of Energy Organization Act, directed the Commission to consider an advance notice of proposed rulemaking on the timely and orderly interconnection of large loads - demand above 20 MW - to the interstate transmission system. Two of the principles put out for comment turn on generation directly: whether large loads and co-located facilities that agree to be flexible and curtail should clear interconnection studies faster, and whether studies could be done in 60 days; and how grid reliability should be evaluated when an existing power plant proposes to shut down in part to serve a new large customer at the same location. The others ask whether large loads should pay the full cost of the grid upgrades their connection needs, and how requests already under review should be treated. This is the instrument the rest of the federal set descends from - the December 2025 PJM order, the June 2026 show cause orders to all six regional transmission organizations, and the July 2026 NERC directive - and it is recorded so the thread starts where it started. The docket page carries a notice extending the comment period and was last updated Jul 22, 2026; no rule has issued. Nothing on this page depends on it and no capacity or consumption figure moves.

head: Generation procured as a backstop, because of large load
body_text: PJM filed this tariff on Jul 31, 2026 under the title Reliability Backstop Procurement to Address Resource Adequacy and Large Loads, asking for it to take effect Sep 29, 2026. The Commission issued its order on that date, accepting the backstop and at the same time opening a companion investigation, Docket EL26-108, into whether parts of it are just and reasonable. Chairman Swett and Commissioners Rosner, See and LaCerte concurred with a separate statement. RTO Insider reported the following day that implementation is suspended for five months while that investigation runs. What makes the order belong in this set is the mechanism rather than the outcome: a regional transmission organization is procuring generation capacity it would not otherwise procure, and the filing's own title names large loads as the reason. It is the operational sibling of the December 2025 co-location order in EL25-49 and the June 2026 show cause orders in EL26-67 through EL26-72, all of which descend from the Department of Energy section 403 directive recorded under RM26-4. No capacity or consumption figure on this page depends on it. The companion investigation has since drawn procedural movement that bears on whether the backstop takes effect. On Oct 13, 2026 PJM filed a Motion for Abeyance under EL26-108 et al. (accession 20261013-5141) and American Municipal Power filed a Request for Clarification and Alternative Request for Rehearing of the Sep 29, 2026 order under ER26-3380 et al. (20261013-5514); Northern Virginia Electric Cooperative answered in support of the abeyance motion on Oct 14, 2026, and on Oct 16, 2026 the Secretary of the Commission issued a Notice Establishing Answer Period (20261016-3047). Three further motions to intervene were docketed on Oct 19, 2026, by the PJM Industrial Customer Coalition, by FirstEnergy and by Duquesne Light Company (20261019-5112), and three more followed: Tract Holding Company I, LLC (20261020-5077) and BlackFlare, Inc. (20261020-5064) on Oct 20, 2026, and an out-of-time motion by Equinix, Inc. on Oct 21, 2026 (20261021-5021). Those are doc-less and procedural. The filing that is not is a joint Motion to Intervene and Protest by Tesla, Inc., Sunrun, Inc. and Renew Home VPP, LLC on Oct 20, 2026 (20261020-5159), directed at the Section 206 investigation itself and the first substantive protest in EL26-108 rather than a bare intervention. Re-read on Oct 21, 2026 the docket sheet carries 35 rows. All of this is read off the eLibrary docket sheet, which was the only accessible source: the filings themselves could not be retrieved in this environment, so nothing is asserted here about PJM's reasoning for seeking abeyance. No figure on this page moves.

head: A generation tariff written for data centers
body_text: Approved by the Governor on Sep 21, 2026 and effective Jan 1, 2027, AB 2383 adds Sections 945.1, 945.4, 945.5, 945.6 and 945.8 to the Public Utilities Code, inside the article that companion bill SB 886 created (Chapter 438, Statutes of 2026). Section 945.5 requires the California Public Utilities Commission to make every electrical corporation file a generation service tariff for data center customers. That tariff must ensure the procurement of generation resources sufficient to meet the commission's procurement requirements and the state's clean energy targets, and must establish a payment mechanism lasting at least ten years under which the data center pays the incremental generation cost increases its own load causes, so that other ratepayers do not carry stranded generation costs. The mechanism has to include early termination fees, upfront collateral or prepayment, and a minimum payment tied to the load stated in the interconnection application; a customer may reduce its obligation only by installing zero-emissions resources behind its own meter. The commission sets the threshold at which the tariff applies and may not set it above 25 megawatts of peak demand. Community choice aggregators and electric service providers must adopt parallel generation tariffs by Jan 1, 2028 under the same cap. This is a statute directing generation procurement against data center load, which is why it is recorded here; it moves no figure on this page.

body: Office of the Governor of Virginia
head: The largest market orders a review of data center backup generation
body_text: Governor Abigail Spanberger signed Executive Order 22 on Sep 18, 2026, creating Virginia's Data Center Accountability Framework in the world's largest data center market. What the order itself does is narrower than the Framework announced around it. The order bans non-disclosure agreements for data center projects across executive branch agencies, boards and authorities, expedites the pending state noise regulations, requires a Data Center Planning and Community Engagement Toolkit for localities within 120 days, and directs a thorough review of diesel and other backup generation operations associated with data centers. That last directive is why this entry is here: a state government is treating data center backup generation as a cumulative source worth measuring. The Framework's generation provisions are not yet law and need the 2027 General Assembly - limiting how much electricity a data center may take from on-site or behind-the-meter gas generation, requiring utilities to allocate a more equitable share of transmission and generation costs to data centers and other large loads, assigning PJM interconnection costs driven by data centers to those data centers, and ending by-right approval for any facility using more than 25 MW. Nothing here moves a figure on this page. It is recorded because the review it commissions is the kind of measurement the generation layer of this map is short of, in the one market that matters most for it.

head: Data centers cut first, and never a critical load
body_text: The Commission approved this Tentative Order 4-0 on Oct 1, 2026, acting on the Sep 10, 2026 motion by Vice Chair Barrow that the Sep 22 news entry recorded while the docket number was still unknown. It is a different docket from the ratemaking working group set up by that same motion, M-2026-3064953. Two proposals are the reason it belongs in this set. First, eligible new large loads that have not secured sufficient new electric capacity to support their demand would be reduced before load is shed from any other customer when PJM calls for reductions under its proposed Interim Resource Adequacy Service, which makes a load's access to firm service turn on whether generation was procured for it. Second, electric distribution companies could no longer classify large loads such as data centers as critical load exempt from curtailment during pre-emergency or emergency events. Utilities would additionally have to build and maintain a registry of large loads in their service territories, which is the first Pennsylvania instrument that would produce a per-territory inventory of this load rather than a tariff for pricing it. The Commission cites its own commissioned Synapse analysis, already recorded in the news block and rejected as an anchor on Test 1 as a consultancy model, finding the regional grid fails PJM's reliability planning standard from 2027 through 2030. Comments run 30 days from publication in the Pennsylvania Bulletin with 15 days for replies, and a Final Order is anticipated at the Jan 28, 2027 public meeting; a Technical Conference on cost allocation for large computational loads is set for Nov 17, 2026. This is curtailment priority rather than generation, so it is recorded on the same footing as Ohio's tariff, Oregon's rate class and the Imperial Irrigation District's Schedule LL, the instrument it most closely resembles. No Pennsylvania metro is mapped on this page, so no capacity or consumption figure depends on it. Read on the Commission's own press release, which states the docket, the 4-0 vote and the four proposed utility obligations. The executed order is now served from the Commission's document system as document 1952506, titled Tentative Order - 3064961 - TUS - 10-1-26 PM - Large Load IRAS, confirmed retrievable on Oct 6, 2026; its text could not be extracted in this environment, so every statement above still rests on the release rather than on the order. Movement since: on Oct 9, 2026 the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission rejected the core of PJM's Interim Resource Adequacy Service in Docket ER26-3515, recorded here as ferc_iras, while accepting the large load registry. The first of this Tentative Order's two proposals is written against an IRAS event, so as of Oct 18, 2026 it rests on a federal framework the Commission has struck down, and the registry obligation is the half of the Pennsylvania order whose federal counterpart survived. The second proposal, barring utilities from classifying large loads as critical load, does not depend on IRAS. Nothing here moves a figure; the docket's Final Order is still anticipated at the Jan 28, 2027 public meeting. That ratemaking docket has since been checked and does not belong in this set: the Order creating the Ratemaking Working Group, from the Sep 10, 2026 public meeting, was posted on Oct 16, 2026 together with a Secretarial Letter of Oct 15, 2026 seeking nominations, and both confine the group's scope to return-on-equity litigation, metrics in rate case settlements and the process for setting the Distribution System Improvement Charge ROE, with data center development named only among the macroeconomic pressures behind the rise in rate filings. Nothing in it prices or inventories large load, so no figure on this page depends on it.

ref: Directive letters to the PUCT and ERCOT (Jun 10 and Aug 3, 2026), to the TWDB (Sep 14, 2026) and to the TCEQ (Sep 21, 2026)
head: No new data center connections until the queue is audited
body_text: Four directive letters from the Governor's office, each read on his own press release. Jun 10, 2026: the PUCT must require data centers to fully fund the electric infrastructure needed to serve them, the PUCT and ERCOT owed a joint memorandum on further ratepayer protections by Jul 17, 2026 and transmission-cost action by Jul 31, 2026, and the release states the aim of legislation making data centers add to the state's electric capacity rather than merely increasing demand. Aug 3, 2026: a comprehensive verification and audit of every data center advancing through ERCOT's interconnection process, which must be completed before any project moves forward, with denial of connection for any project that does not comply. The audit collects, project by project, projected annual and peak electricity consumption and any effort and progress to construct or procure on-site electric generation including generation type, alongside state and local financial assistance, water sources and cooling technology, community mitigation measures and ownership. That generation question is why this entry belongs in this set: a state is compiling, per project, how much of this load intends to bring its own generation. The same release puts ERCOT's interconnection requests at roughly 474 GW, more than five times the record ERCOT peak, about 90 percent of them data centers; that is a queue figure rather than capacity and nothing on this page is drawn from it. Sep 14, 2026: the TWDB to compel water-use reporting from major water users including data centers, with civil and criminal consequences for failure, and to partner with ERCOT on the audit. Sep 21, 2026: the TCEQ to halt all permits sought by data centers until the audit completes, with a compliance update to the Governor due Oct 19, 2026. The Aug 3 letter sets no deadline for the audit itself. Texas SB6, already recorded here, is the statute; these are executive directives that have paused approvals under it, and they are recorded on the same footing as Massachusetts Executive Order 658 and Virginia Executive Order 22. No capacity or consumption figure on this page moves: the mapped Dallas-Fort Worth inventory and the mapped Texas campuses are already energized or already announced, and a pause on new approvals does not change them.

head: New plant approved, by the megawatt, for one data center
body_text: The Commission approved two special contracts between DTE Electric and Google for a data center in Van Buren Township, Wayne County: a primary supply agreement governing electric service, and a clean capacity accelerator agreement under which Google pays for DTE Electric to develop up to 1,600 MW of renewable energy and 480 MW of battery energy storage, developed, owned and operated by the utility, to help power that one facility. The second instrument is why this entry is here. Every other generation-linked filing in this set either obliges a data center to bring generation of its own or sets the terms on which it may connect to someone else's; here a state commission approves specific new plant, with a megawatt figure attached, built because one customer asked for it and billed to that customer. The supply agreement runs 20 years against the 5 years DTE Electric's general large-load D11 rate requires, sets minimum billing demand at 80% against 50-65% in D11, and adds an early termination payment covering at least 15 years of minimum monthly charges plus credit and collateral requirements. According to DTE Electric the data center is expected to begin taking service in December 2027 and to reach maximum load by December 2028. The Commission states its authority runs only to the terms of the contracts, not to whether or where a data center may locate. No Michigan metro is mapped on this page and the Van Buren Township site is not in the campus layer, so no figure here depends on it; the 1,600 MW is generation rather than IT capacity and is counted nowhere on this page. Read on the Commission's own release; the order itself was not retrieved.

body: Black Hills Corp., under the Wyoming Large Power Contract Service tariff
ref: Large Power Contract Services Agreement and Generation Facilities Agreement, effective Sep 30, 2026
head: 564 MW of new gas plant contracted for one data center
body_text: Black Hills Corp. announced on Oct 6, 2026 that it had executed two agreements, effective Sep 30, 2026 and running through 2048, to serve a planned Google data center in Cheyenne, Wyoming: a Large Power Contract Services Agreement and a Generation Facilities Agreement, both under the company's Wyoming Large Power Contract Service tariff. Black Hills will invest $1.8 billion between 2027 and 2029 to build 564 MW of nameplate company-owned gas-fired generation at its existing Cheyenne Prairie site, provide up to 590 MW of grid-connected energy service, and manage about 2.1 GW of Wyoming-based third-party contracted resources through a privately managed microgrid, for a stated total resource mix of about 2.7 GW including reserve margins. Service is planned to begin in late 2027 and to ramp to peak load in 2030. This sits beside the Michigan DTE Electric contracts as the second instrument in this set where specific new plant, with a megawatt figure attached, is built because one data center asked for it and billed to that customer. The difference is provenance: the Michigan plant was approved by a state commission, while here the generating units are to be owned by a non-regulated Black Hills affiliate rather than the Wyoming utility, an air quality permit for the Cheyenne Prairie expansion is secured, and siting and transmission approvals are still being pursued. Nothing on the map moves on this. The 2.7 GW is a power resource mix including reserve margins, not mapped IT capacity, and no IT capacity figure has been published for the planned Google campus at Cheyenne, so the campus list is unchanged. No Wyoming Public Service Commission docket for the agreements appeared in any source reached on Oct 9, 2026.

ref: Docket No. 60332, Application of Southwestern Public Service Company for Approval of Large Load Customer Tariff Provisions
head: A Texas large-load tariff that bills new generation to the data center
body_text: Southwestern Public Service Company, Xcel Energy's Texas utility, applied to the Public Utility Commission of Texas on Sep 25, 2026 for approval of large load customer tariff provisions, docketed as 60332 after a request for a docket number filed the day before. Xcel's own announcement of Sep 28, 2026 states what the tariff would do: large electricity users such as data centers would be subject to commercial terms and customer commitments making them responsible for the cost of the electric transmission, substations, interconnection upgrades and new generation required to serve their projects, on commitments typically of 15 years or more backed by financial security provisions if a project is delayed, scaled back or not completed, with minimum monthly payment requirements while load ramps gradually and termination charges designed to recover project-specific infrastructure costs if a customer leaves service early. The docket is contested and moving: Texas Industrial Energy Consumers moved to intervene on Sep 29, 2026, AXM on Oct 1, the Commission issued Order No. 1 on Oct 2 requiring Commission Staff comments and granting AXM's intervention, Staff filed comments on the application, the proposed notice and the proposed procedural schedule on Oct 9, 2026, and on Oct 12, 2026 the Commission issued Order No. 2, granting a motion to intervene and addressing other procedural matters, and Order No. 3, finding the application administratively complete and the proposed notice sufficient and entering a procedural schedule. On Oct 16, 2026 the Office of Public Utility Counsel, the statutory representative of Texas residential and small commercial consumers, filed its own motion to intervene, taking the docket sheet to 13 filings against 12 on Oct 12, 2026 and 10 on Oct 9, 2026; it was still 13 when re-read on Oct 17, Oct 18, Oct 19 and Oct 20, 2026. Two further filings carry a file stamp of Oct 20, 2026 and took the sheet to 15 when it was re-read on Oct 21, 2026: a motion to intervene by Targa Resources Corp., and a First Request for Information to Southwestern Public Service Company from Texas Industrial Energy Consumers. The second is the first discovery in the docket, which moves it from pleadings into the procedural schedule entered by Order No. 3. This is the third Texas instrument in this set, beside Senate Bill 6 and the Governor's directive letters, and the first that assigns the cost of new generation to the large customer by tariff rather than by statute or by a single negotiated contract. Nothing on the map moves on it. SPS serves the Texas Panhandle and South Plains, where this page maps no metro; Dallas-Fort Worth, the only mapped Texas metro, is not in its territory, and no IT capacity figure is involved. The filed documents themselves were not read: the PUCT document server is unreachable from this session, so every statement above rests on the docket sheet's own record of parties, dates, item types and filing descriptions, and on Xcel Energy's published description of its own proposal.

ref: Docket ER26-3515-000, order of Oct 9, 2026, eLibrary accession 20261009-3055
head: Connecting a data center without generation for it: rejected
body_text: PJM Interconnection filed this tariff on Aug 13, 2026 under the title Proposal to Establish Interim Resource Adequacy Service and a Large Load Registry, asking for an effective date of Oct 12, 2026. On Oct 9, 2026 the Commission issued an Order Accepting Tariff Revisions in Part and Rejecting Tariff Revisions in Part, with Commissioner Rosner concurring in a separate statement. What belongs in this set is the mechanism the order turns on. Interim Resource Adequacy Service, or IRAS, would have let an eligible new large load connect without matching new capacity provided it agreed to be curtailed ahead of a grid emergency, together with bring-your-own-new-capacity rules: that is a tariff making a data center's access to firm service turn on whether generation was procured for it. The Commission accepted PJM's definition of large loads and its large load registry, which would record each facility's location, ramp schedule and capacity supply, and rejected the IRAS package that formed the core of the filing, finding that several provisions appear to place obligations directly on retail customers, to dictate which retail customers taking retail service will be curtailed, and to establish a retail rate through the proposed compensation framework, and that they appear to discriminate against large loads. It is the second rejection in five weeks of a PJM instrument aimed at this load, after the Sep 29, 2026 order on the Reliability Backstop Procurement recorded here under Dockets ER26-3380 and EL26-108. Nothing on the map moves on it: the order sets no megawatt figure and no capacity or consumption figure on this page depends on it. The order document itself is a public DOCX in eLibrary that could not be extracted in this environment, so the docket, date, accession, filing title, requested effective date and the accepted-in-part, rejected-in-part disposition rest on the eLibrary docket sheet and file list read on Oct 18, 2026, and the quoted findings and the substance of the accepted-versus-rejected split on Utility Dive's report of Oct 12, 2026, which quotes the order directly. The newest activity on the docket as of Oct 21, 2026 is a Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission service-list update of Oct 15, 2026; no request for rehearing or compliance filing has appeared.

ref: Proceeding No. 26AL-0137E (Advice Letter No. 2018, Tariff 8 - Large Load), opened Apr 2, 2026, status Suspended
head: Colorado puts Xcel's large load tariff to hearing
body_text: Public Service Company of Colorado, Xcel Energy's Colorado utility, filed Advice Letter No. 2018 on Apr 2, 2026, proposing a Tariff 8 large load schedule. The Commission suspended the advice letter and set it down for hearing, which is why the proceeding's status on the Commission's own e-filings system still reads Suspended. What puts it in this set is the same mechanism the Texas, Pennsylvania, Ohio and Oregon entries turn on: a tariff that decides how much of the cost of serving a very large new load, and of the generation and network built for it, is carried by that customer rather than by everyone else on the system. The docket is contested and the parties are the ones that mark these cases out. The Data Center Coalition, the industry's own trade association, filed an affidavit supporting direct testimony on Oct 20, 2026; United Power, an electric cooperative, moved on Oct 16, 2026 for leave to file a second revised answer testimony, which Public Service Company objected to on Oct 20, 2026; Ceres filed two sets of comments on Oct 20, 2026, one of them on the water implications of the proposed tariff; 350 Colorado filed comments on Oct 19, 2026; and public comment has been arriving daily through the hearing week. The newest Commission document on the sheet is a Hearing Report stamped Oct 20, 2026. Nothing on the map moves on it. Denver is mapped, at 78 MW of live IT capacity on a 2023 Cushman & Wakefield vintage, but this is a cost-allocation tariff and it sets no megawatt figure; Colorado publishes no measured data center electricity series, so no anchor depends on the outcome either. The proceeding number, title, open date, status, and the filing titles, dates and parties above are read off the Commission's e-filings proceeding sheet on Oct 21, 2026. The filed documents themselves were not retrieved in this environment, so nothing is asserted here about what any party argued; the reported evidentiary hearing dates of Oct 21, 22, 26, 27 and 28, 2026 rest on Colorado press reports and not on the docket sheet.

ref: Dockets 20260146-EI (Tampa Electric Company), 20260148-EI (Florida Public Utilities Company) and 20260149-EI (Florida Power & Light Company), opened Sep 30 to Oct 1, 2026
head: Florida's utilities file large load tariffs under a new statute
body_text: Three Florida electric utilities opened large load tariff dockets at the Florida Public Service Commission within two days of each other. Tampa Electric Company docketed 20260146-EI on Sep 30, 2026, a petition for approval of large load customer tariffs. Florida Public Utilities Company docketed 20260148-EI on Oct 1, 2026, a petition for authority to implement a large load service tariff. Florida Power & Light Company docketed 20260149-EI on Oct 1, 2026, a petition for approval of a limited tariff revision and to find that its existing large load contract service tariff is in compliance, and that docket title cites Section 366.043(8), Florida Statutes, which is what ties the three filings together. Florida press reports that statute as SB 484, signed in May 2026, requiring the Commission to set tariffs and service requirements so that each large load customer bears its own full cost of service rather than shifting it to the general body of ratepayers, the cost of generation and transmission included; the statutory citation is read off the docket title, the bill number and its history are not. What puts Florida in this set is the mechanism the Texas, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Oregon and Colorado entries turn on: a tariff deciding how much of the cost of the generation built for a very large new load is carried by that customer rather than by everyone else on the system. Nothing on the map moves on it. No Florida metro is mapped, so no capacity figure is touched, and Florida publishes no measured data center electricity series, so no anchor depends on the outcome. The docket numbers, docketing dates, filing companies and official docket titles above are read off the Commission Clerk's Office Report of New Dockets Opened for the week of Sep 28 to Oct 2, 2026, on Oct 22, 2026. The filed petitions themselves were not retrieved in this environment, so nothing is asserted here about what any utility proposed beyond the titles the Clerk recorded.

ref: Dockets 26-04026 and 26-04027 (Utility Environmental Protection Act permits, granted Sep 17, 2026, reconsideration pending), 26-06016 (permit, hearing held Oct 21, 2026), and 26-05026 to 26-05030 (Large Load Electric Service Agreements, pending)
head: Nevada permits two large loads to build their own gas generation
body_text: Nevada is in this set for the plainest version of the mechanism the whole set is about: a very large new electrical load building its own generation. On Apr 20, 2026 two companies applied to the Public Utilities Commission of Nevada, under the Utility Environmental Protection Act, for permits to construct gas plants on private land in Storey County. PR RNO Property Owner 1, LLC sought the Peru Ridge Self-Generation Project, a temporary 218 MW natural gas-fueled generating facility, in docket 26-04027; SV RNO Property Owner 1 LLC sought the South Valley Temporary Power Generation Facility, a temporary 144 MW gas facility, in docket 26-04026. The Commission granted both on Sep 17, 2026, after a hearing on Aug 11, 2026 and a draft order on Sep 11, 2026 on the 26-04027 sheet. Both grants are under challenge: the Bureau of Consumer Protection petitioned for reconsideration on Oct 1, 2026 and filed again on Oct 2, 2026 jointly with a party the Commission's sheet records as NCARE; the two applicants answered on Oct 14, 2026 and Commission Staff on Oct 15, 2026, and neither docket shows a ruling on reconsideration. What ties the generation to the load is the Commission's own docket titles rather than any inference drawn here: the same two companies, PR RNO Property Owner 1, LLC and SV RNO Property Owner 1, LLC, are the named customers in Sierra Pacific Power Company's application for approval of Large Load Electric Service Agreements, docket 26-05027, filed May 29, 2026 and still at Procedural Order No. 1 of Jul 22, 2026. That large load docket is one of a cluster of five filed in the same week, and the other four name data center operators outright: Amazon Data Services in 26-05026, Vantage Data Centers NV11 in 26-05028, Novva Las Vegas and Proton NLV in 26-05029, and VIP LANDCO and Prologis through Nevada Power in 26-05030. The Bureau of Consumer Protection intervened in each on Jun 3, 2026 and the customers themselves intervened on Jul 1, 2026. A third gas permit is pending in the same county and is explicitly inside the data center cluster: Nexus Fulcrum LLC's application for ASR-IX, a nominal 510 MW natural gas-fueled plant within the Tahoe Reno Industrial Center complex, docket 26-06016, filed Jun 17, 2026, which drew public comments on Oct 13, 14 and 15, 2026 and went to hearing on Oct 21, 2026 with no decision on the sheet. Nothing on the map moves on any of it. Las Vegas / Reno is mapped at 173 MW of live IT capacity on a 2023 Cushman & Wakefield vintage and Google Storey County at 161 MW, but a generation permit is not IT capacity and a service agreement sets no megawatt figure for the map; Nevada publishes no measured data center electricity series, so no anchor depends on the outcome either. The docket numbers, official titles, filing dates, document types and order dates above are read off the Commission's All Dockets sheet and its public document search on Oct 24, 2026. The filed applications, orders and reconsideration petitions were not retrieved in this environment, so nothing is asserted here about what any party argued, and the docket titles do not state what load the Peru Ridge and South Valley plants are built to serve.
